newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Merrill Lynch sees Slovak crown weakening in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Merrill Lynch sees Slovak crown weakening in 1997.

text.p: The Slovak crown is expected to weaken by around four percent within its set fluctuation band this year from current near-parity levels against its mark/dollar basket, Merrill Lynch said in its latest Slovak research report.

"At present, we forecast the crown to weaken gradually to around four percent cheap (below parity) in its band this year," Merrill Lynch International said in its report made available to Reuters on Wednesday. Merrill said the currency appeared "unlikely" to be forced out of its set corridor of plus/minus seven percent against parity with a mark/dollar basket in 1997, given the central bank's ability and willingness to support the currency.
But Merrill Lynch advised investors to be cautious.

"We advise caution on investing in Slovakia. In particular, longer-term investors should be concerned by the widening current account deficit, which could increase the rate of (the) crown's depreciation later in the year."
Merrill Lynch said it estimated the 1997 Slovak current account deficit could widen to more than 12 percent of gorss domestic product (GDP), up from an estimated 10 percent of GDP in 1996.

"More worrying" was the shift in the composition of the capital account towards short-term capital, which covered the current account shortfall and kept foreign exchange reserves stable in 1996, Merrill said.
"Large movements of short-term capital are likely to make the crown increasingly vulnerable to market sentiment this year," it said.
But the report said central bank reserves should be sufficient to support the crown during the outflow of short-term money.
Merrill noted currency forwards and Euro-Slovak crown investments remain "reasonably attractive" with returns of over 11.5 percent.
The crown's depreciation of 3 to 5 percent would imply returns of 200-450 basis points after funding costs, the report said.
